summary: The flow matches its sources on who creates tasks, lane isolation, integration gates and the authorized squash merge. Nine claims about slots, topology.json, worktree-before-claim, ORCH UPDATE and the ff-only stop rule are true but stated only in skills/loop.md and docs/agents-detail.md, which the spec does not list as sources. The most important factual gaps are QA shown as a step of the queued feature chain, "evidence" shown as a queue.db field, and the missing "not authorized" path at the merge gate.

code.overview: About half of this flow is code, and nearly all of it is the queue CLI: scripts/queue.ts with queue-task-origin.ts, queue-claim.ts, queue-worktrees.ts, queue-lanes.ts and queue-delivery.ts, plus scripts/topology.ts for the slots. The code records who owns which task and refuses out-of-order moves. Choosing a slot, starting the subagent, merging the target into the lane, merging the lane, opening the PR and the squash merge are all done by the agent from prose; the code never merges or pushes.

refs.anchor: if (parent && !q.tasks.some(t => t.id === parent)) return { ok: false, error: `queue add: --parent ${parent} is not a task in this queue` };
refs.title: taskOrigin: refuse an agent's add without the owner's words
refs.explain: It reads the --parent and --requested flags. An unknown parent id is an error. With neither flag, it checks the environment for agent markers such as CLAUDECODE or CODEX_THREAD_ID: an agent session is refused with the AGENT_ADD_REFUSAL message, a human passes. Otherwise it returns tags and a note that record the parent or the quoted request on the task.
refs.why: This is the check behind 'only the owner creates tasks'. Without it an agent could grow the backlog with its own ideas. The comment at the top of the file notes the quote is not authenticated, so this is a guardrail, not proof.

refs.anchor: if (!title) { console.error('usage: queue add "<title>" [--parent <id> | --requested "<human words>"] [flags]'); return 1; }
refs.title: queue add: record one task
refs.explain: The title is the joined positional words; an empty title prints usage and exits 1. taskOrigin decides whether the add is allowed, and a refusal exits 2. addTask appends the task (or puts it first with --top) with the flags and origin tags merged in. save writes the store, the log gets an 'add' line, and the new id is printed with a drain hint.
refs.why: This is the entry point of the flow: the owner's request becomes a typed task with an id. Skipping it leaves the request only in chat, where no later step can find it.

refs.anchor: export function loadTopology(path: string = process.env.TOPOLOGY_FILE ?? TOPOLOGY_PATH): Topology {
refs.title: parseTopology and loadTopology: read the worker slots
refs.explain: parseTopology rejects anything that is not an object or has unknown keys, checks the orchestrator model, defaults tick_minutes to 10 and requires it to be positive, then parses the slots. loadTopology reads .agent/topology.json (or TOPOLOGY_FILE); a missing file means an orchestrator with no slots, and bad JSON throws a TopologyError.
refs.why: Dispatch starts by reading the slots from this file. The file has no routing fields on purpose: which task suits which slot is the orchestrator's judgment, not code.

refs.anchor: + `First step in the lane: \`git merge --ff-only ${base}\` (a reused branch may be stale); stop if it cannot fast-forward. `
refs.title: queue worktree add: create the lane
refs.explain: The base is config.integrationBranch, else the current branch. It runs git worktree add at .agent/queue/wt/<id> on a new branch queue/<id>; if that branch already exists it reuses it. It saves the branch and worktree path on the task, logs the base commit, and prints the lane's first step: git merge --ff-only <base>.
refs.why: This creates the isolated lane off the working branch before the task is claimed. The ff-only check and the merge back are only printed as instructions; the comment says the CLI never auto-merges.

refs.anchor: export function cmdClaim(q: Queue, id: string, flags: Map<string, string>, taskBlock: (t: Task) => string): number {
refs.title: queue claim: give a pending task to a worker or slot
refs.explain: refusal rejects a task that is not pending, is held, or is blocked by an unfinished delivery cycle. branchFlag rejects a --branch value that is not one name. The worker name comes from --worker, else a name built from the process id. One save marks the task active with that owner and, when given, links the branch in the same write.
refs.why: This is how a slot takes a task: the task's owner becomes the slot id. Linking the branch in the same write means a task is never active with an unlinked branch.

refs.anchor: export function slotViews(q: Queue, topology: Topology, lanes: LaneView[] = []): { slots: SlotView[]; orphans: ConsoleOrphan[] } {
refs.title: slotViews: which slots are busy
refs.explain: It takes the active tasks and, for each topology slot, picks those whose owner equals the slot id. A slot with one or more is busy; with more than one it is flagged overbooked. Active tasks owned by no known slot are returned as orphans.
refs.why: A free slot is defined as 'no active task owned by this slot id', so the claim's --worker value is what marks a slot busy. This view feeds the console's Slots panel; the dispatch decision itself is still made by the agent.

refs.anchor: t.mode === 'chain' ? 'mode: chain (design→prd→plan→tdd→refine, autonomous, no questions)' : 'mode: direct',
refs.title: taskBlock: the task text a worker receives
refs.explain: It builds a list of lines from the task: the mode (chain or direct), the architecture mode and its guidance, the docs slug, the accept note, files, contracts and the validate command. Empty lines are dropped and the result is wrapped in a <queue_task id=...> block. tick and claim print this block.
refs.why: This is how the subagent learns whether to build a chore directly or run the full design-to-refine chain, and what counts as accepted. Following those steps is then up to the agent.

refs.anchor: if (!id || !q.tasks.some(t => t.id === id)) { console.error(`lane ${sub}: unknown task id`); return 1; }
refs.title: queue lane finish: the subagent reports done and keeps its claim
refs.explain: The first part of cmdLane lists lane heartbeat files, marking stale ones and stop requests. For 'finish' it requires the task to be active and --worker to match the task's owner, then writes the lane file with state awaiting-review and logs that root review is required. The task itself stays active.
refs.why: The subagent reports and stops; it does not mark its own task done or merge. The claim stays in place until the orchestrator reviews the lane.

refs.anchor: /** Run a task's validation command; the worktree (if any) is the working dir. */
refs.title: runValidate: run the task's validate command in its worktree
refs.explain: No validate command means success. Otherwise the command runs with the task's worktree as its working directory when one is recorded. A non-zero exit returns failure with the last three lines of output.
refs.why: The task's own gate runs against the lane's files, not the orchestrator's checkout. Without the worktree cwd a lane's work could be judged by code that is not in it.

refs.title: CI verify job: npm test on every PR to main
refs.explain: On a pull request to main, the job checks out the code without stored credentials, installs the Node version from .node-version, runs npm ci and then npm test. npm test chains the node tests, the tool tests, the shell tests and the repo checks.
refs.why: These are the 'real check results' the orchestrator reads after it opens the PR. The earlier half of this stage (merge the target into the lane, re-run gates locally, merge the lane) has no code; the agent does it from the rules.

refs.anchor: console.error('advance: requires selected completed task, no active claims, --pr <merged-pr-url> and --branch <fresh-working-branch>');
refs.title: queue advance: record the merged PR and the fresh branch
refs.explain: It refuses unless the id is the selected delivery task, that task was accepted as done, no task is active, --pr looks like a pull request URL and --branch is not empty. On success it clears deliveryTask and deliveryAccepted, saves, and writes the PR and branch to the log.
refs.why: This closes the delivery cycle so the queue will hand out the next task. The code checks only the queue's own state and the URL's shape; it does not ask GitHub whether the PR merged, so the orchestrator vouches for that.

refs.title: Release job: tag main after the merge
refs.explain: On a push to main it checks out full history and reads the version from package.json. If the tag v<version> already exists it stops. Otherwise it creates the annotated tag and pushes only the tag.
refs.why: This is the only code that runs because of the merge. It relies on the version bump already being on the PR branch, and it pushes a tag, never a commit, so main's history stays one squash commit per PR.
